q: Multi-tape Turing machines can recognise languages that single-tape Turing machines cannot.
explain: False. A single tape can simulate k tapes side by side. Multi-tape machines are faster, but not more powerful.

q: A k-tape TM runs for t steps. Simulating it on a single-tape TM takes about…
explain: Each simulated step sweeps over the used part of the single tape, which is O(t) long. Over t steps that gives O(t²).

q: A nondeterministic TM accepts w when…
options: at least one branch of its computation accepts
the first branch it tries accepts
explain: As with NFAs and PDAs, nondeterministic acceptance needs just one successful branch.

q: To simulate an NDTM, a deterministic TM should explore the computation tree…
explain: Depth-first could follow an infinite branch forever and miss an accepting branch elsewhere. Breadth-first finds any accepting branch at a finite depth.

q: Nondeterministic Turing machines recognise exactly the same languages as deterministic ones.
explain: True. The breadth-first simulation shows it, though the simulation may take exponentially more time.

q: The deterministic simulation of an NDTM with branching factor b, accepting at depth t, can take time about…
explain: There can be up to bᵗ branches at depth t. Whether this blow-up is avoidable is essentially the P vs NP question.

q: Which models are equivalent in power to a standard Turing machine?
options: A TM with a semi-infinite tape
explain: Two stacks can simulate a tape (one stack for each side of the head). A PDA with one stack only reaches the context-free languages.

q: In a multi-tape TM, the head moves are usually chosen from {L, R, S}. What does S mean?
options: Stay: the head does not move
explain: S lets a head stay where it is while the others move. It adds convenience, not power.

q: Which task does the 'guess and check' style of an NDTM suit?
options: Deciding whether n is composite: guess a factor, then check that it divides n
Reading the input once from left to right
explain: Nondeterminism shines when a solution is hard to find but easy to verify, which is the hallmark of NP.

q: That so many different models (multi-tape, nondeterministic, two-stack, λ-calculus, real languages) all compute the same functions is evidence for…
explain: Every reasonable formalisation of 'algorithm' turns out equivalent to Turing machines. That robustness is the main argument for the thesis.
